newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean strikes ease as nurses, drivers back down.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean strikes ease as nurses, drivers back down.

text.p: Strikes crippling South Korean industry showed signs of easing on Monday as subway drivers returned to work and nurses prepared to back down.

But militant union leaders insisted members were only temporarily retreating to spare the public from chaos over the New Year holiday and that industrial action would resume with a vengeance next year.
Figures issued by the government indicated the number of strikers was falling, although major shipyards and car plants were still idle.

The government maintained its uncompromising stand. The cabinet on Monday approved a new labour bill that was passed by the National Assembly last Thursday, sparking a wave of strikes across the nation.
Train drivers and engineers on subways in Seoul and South Korea's second largest city, Pusan, returned to duty on Monday morning after a two-day walkout.
Their strikes had caused only minor delays as non-union workers kept train services running.
Nurses and hospital orderlies agreed to return to work on Tuesday. At one point, 17 hospitals, including Seoul National University Hospital, offered emergency treatment only.
Monday's climb-down followed a weekend of rallies during which workers besieged the headquarters of the ruling New Korea Party in Seoul and fought running battles with riot police.
But union leaders remained defiant and said industrial action would be resumed at a new level of intensity after the holidays.
"We will take our strikes to a higher level and prolong them starting in the new year," said Kwon Young-kil, leader of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
"We will demand the resignation of Lee Soo-sung's entire cabinet," he said, referring to the prime minister.
By Saturday, unions claimed 375,000 workers had downed tools out of a total unionised workforce of 1.7 million. The labour ministry said fewer than 100,000 were off work.
In a televised address, prime minister Lee defended the labour law, which allows companies to lay off workers, employ temorary staff and replace strikers.
"We chose the law to prevent our offspring from falling behind developing countries and suffering in a devastating swamp," Lee said.
"We could not watch companies go bankrupt and corporations move offshore, causing major job losses."

The largest umbrella union body, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, met on Monday to decide whether to prolong a stoppage called initially until the end of the year. There was no immediate word on the outcome.
Separately, union workers at Korea Telecom, the state telecommunications giant, were voting on whether to join the industrial action.
Bank tellers and clerks have voted to strike for one day next Saturday.
The central bank said strikes would help swell South Korea's current account deficit this year to more than $22 billion from its earlier forecast of about $21.5 billion.

"Traditionally, we've seen strong exports at the year end. But that's unlikely to be the case this year with labour strikes hindering exports during the last week of this month," said bank official Paeng Dong-joon.
"At this point, the current account deficit is seen well above $22 billion for the year."
